text: You walk into a temple. A fifty-yuan ticket, three sticks of complimentary incense—but the stillness of that day was real.
The first incense of New Year's Eve sold for sixty-eight thousand. Watching from outside the crowd, you couldn't tell if this was faith or an auction.
You dropped ten yuan into the merit box. The kind of giving that asks nothing in return. That night, you slept unexpectedly deeply.
A bracelet 'blessed by a master' for three thousand eight hundred. Six months later you saw the same one at a wholesale market—9.9 yuan, free shipping.
You volunteered at the monastery—sweeping floors, picking vegetables, pointing pilgrims the right way. Physical labor, it turned out, cures spiritual exhaustion.
The day you took refuge, you received your Dharma name. The master said: faith is not asking, it is learning to let go. You half-understood—but you remembered.
The fortune-teller at the alley corner said your brow was clouded with ill luck, and offered to read your fortune for fifty yuan. You laughed—but you sat down anyway.

'This reading only covered your fate, not your fortune.' The master said changing your luck would cost extra—eighteen hundred. In those three seconds of hesitation, every misfortune you'd ever had came back to you.
'Your daughter faces a blood calamity soon.' The 'senior mentor' on the livestream says only spending money can ward it off—the course is just 3,999.
It took the police showing up at your door for you to understand: the master's 'divine accuracy' came from your ID number, passed along by the receptionist at the beauty salon.
The afternoon your savings hit bottom, you threw the 'luck-reversal talisman' into the trash. The bin was full—your life still had half a glass left.
You sat down in the fortune-teller's booth yourself. The first time you cheated someone out of their money, your hands shook; by the tenth, they were steady—and that keeps you up at night.
The plainclothes officers flashed their badges while you were reading someone's 'blood calamity.' The case involved over twenty million—and you were the lowest rung in the crew.
The qigong master claimed a blade could slice tumors out through the air, at a million a month. Desperate people will believe anything once.
The master was sentenced to twelve years. Watching the blade props on the news, you touched your own surgery scar, still not fully healed.
The 'quantum fluctuation speed-reading' class cost twenty-six thousand—children flipping through books blindfolded. You asked one question in the parents' group chat and got removed.
The day the kids blew the scam wide open in public, the training center vanished with the money. You stood in the middle of the restitution line—four hundred parents ahead of you.
At a late-night food stall, the college student at the next table moved from Zi Wei astrology to the fall of the Roman Empire. You listened, stunned: was he a prophet, or a patient?
You met that 'knower of heaven and earth' again. This time he was sorting through a psychiatry medicine box—so both explanations were right all along.
It was bitterly cold the day your head was shaved. The master asked why you came; you said you wanted a place that wouldn't collapse. He said: this place collapses too—what collapses is attachment.
Morning prayers at four a.m. Some dawn three hundred days later, you suddenly realized it had been a long time since your last nightmare.
Your mother came to visit and wept across the dining-hall table. The hand you offered tissues with was steady—so steady it made her cry even harder.
You returned to the secular world. Carrying ten years of stillness, you walked into the subway station, where the sound of the crowd was like the sea of another planet.
